newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua central bank head sees economic take-off.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua central bank head sees economic take-off.

text.p: Nicaragua's annual gross domestic product of about $2 billion will grow by at least 5.5 percent in 1996 and from 6.5 percent to 7.0 percent in 1997, Nicaraguan Central Bank President Jose Evenor Taboada said on Tuesday.

Taboada painted a rosy picture of the Nicaraguan economy after the six years of deep structural reforms carried out by the centrist, free-market government of President Violeta Chamorro, who was voted to power in 1990, ending nearly 11 years of Marxist Sandinista government.
Chamorro will hand over power to right-wing President- elect Arnoldo Aleman on January 190.

"The prospects for 1996 and the conditions for 1997 are extraordinarily good. We expect to continue with the lowest inflation rate in Central America, and there is a clear trend towards falling unemployment," Taboada said on the morning television talk show In Depth.
Inflation is expected to run near 11 percent in 1996.
He said the process of structural adjustment and building a free-market economy in Nicaragua is now almost complete, bringing monetary stability and making Nicaragua more attractive to investors.

Taboada also praised the government's debt reduction program, which has chopped Nicaragua's debt from $10.344 billion in 1990 to $5.517 billion today, thanks mainly to debt forgiveness by countries such as Russia and Germany, which assumed huge Sandinista debts run up with the former Soviet Union and East Germany.

But Nicaragua still has a long road to climb after years of economic decline. Back-to-back civil wars against the dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza in the 1970s and the Sandinista government in the 1980s took an economic toll.

Combined unemployment and underemployment stands at 53 percent of the workforce, according to the Central Bank, and non-governmental organizations say 70 percent of Nicaraguans live below the poverty line.
A 1996 U.N. study puts Nicaragua as the least developed country in Latin America after Haiti.
Nicaragua began to see some light at the end of the tunnel in 1994 when the economy grew by 3.3 percent, followed by four percent growth in 1995.
Taboada said the challenge facing Nicaragua now is to wean itself off foreign assistance and on to internal savings.
"We have to accept as a reality that in the medium term external resources are going to decline," he said.
He said international backers have assured Nicaragua $1.5 billion in aid over the next three years, easing the short-term sting, but that this will not last.

"In the short term, fortunately, we can count on international solidarity, but we must be aware that we must become independent of this international cooperation if we are to build a solid economy," he said.
